l: Toto, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter III
s: Toto accompanies Dorothy, drinks from the brook, barks at birds, and attracts the curiosity of the Munchkins, who have never seen a dog. He initially growls at the Scarecrow and suspects there may be rats in the straw, but Dorothy says he never bites.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter III
s: The Great Oz is the person Dorothy plans to ask for help in returning to Kansas. The Scarecrow also hopes Oz may give him brains.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter III
s: The Emerald City is Dorothy's destination. Dorothy follows the yellow brick road toward it, and Boq warns that it is a long way away and that dangerous places lie along the journey.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter III
s: Kansas is Dorothy's home country, to which she wants to return. She hopes the Great Oz can tell her how to get back there.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter III
s: The Scarecrow is a stuffed figure placed on a pole to scare birds from a cornfield. He can speak and move, but he says he has no brains and wants to ask the Great Oz for some. Dorothy removes him from the pole and takes him along toward the Emerald City; he can carry her basket without getting tired and is afraid only of a lighted match.

l: the road of yellow brick, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter III
s: The yellow brick road leads Dorothy toward the Emerald City. She finds it near the Munchkin homes and travels along it with Toto, later joined by the Scarecrow.

l: Silver Shoes, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter III
s: The silver shoes belonged to the Witch of the East. Dorothy tries them on, finds that they fit perfectly, and wears them for the journey because she believes they cannot wear out; they tinkle as she walks.

l: brains, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter III
s: The Scarecrow believes he has no brains because his head is stuffed with straw. He wants the Great Oz to give him brains so that people will not call him a fool and so that he can know things.

l: journey to the Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter III
s: Dorothy begins the journey with Toto after preparing food, water, clothing, and the silver shoes. She spends one night with the Munchkins, continues along the yellow brick road, and adds the Scarecrow to her party after rescuing him from his pole.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: Dorothy and the Scarecrow travel along the increasingly rough yellow brick road toward the Emerald City. During a rest, Dorothy tells the Scarecrow about Kansas and the cyclone that brought her to the Land of Oz, while he explains how he was made and why he wants brains from the Great Oz. They enter a dark forest and find a log-and-branch cottage where Dorothy sleeps while the Scarecrow keeps watch.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: Dorothy travels with the Scarecrow and Toto along the rough yellow brick road. She tells the Scarecrow about Kansas and says that people would rather live in their own homes than in any other country. She enters a cottage in the forest and sleeps on dried leaves.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: The Scarecrow often falls into holes in the uneven road, but Dorothy helps him up and he laughs at his mishaps. He explains that he was made only two days earlier, wants brains, and believes the Great Oz will give them to him. He leads Dorothy to a cottage in the forest and waits there through the night.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: Kansas is described by Dorothy as a dry, gray place with dreary homes. Although it is less beautiful than the Land of Oz, Dorothy says that people of flesh and blood would rather live there because there is no place like home.

l: Land of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: The Land of Oz is described as beautiful compared with Kansas. Dorothy was carried there by the cyclone.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: The Emerald City is the destination at the end of the yellow brick road. The Scarecrow and Dorothy continue through the forest because they believe the road leads there.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: The Scarecrow believes the Great Oz will give him brains when they reach the Emerald City.

l: the road of yellow brick, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: The yellow brick road becomes rough and uneven, with broken or missing bricks and holes. It eventually leads Dorothy and the Scarecrow into a great forest.

l: forest, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: The forest has very large, closely spaced trees whose branches meet over the yellow brick road. It becomes dark as the travelers proceed, and they find a small cottage where Dorothy spends the night.

l: the cyclone, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: The cyclone carried Dorothy from Kansas to the Land of Oz.

l: brains, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: The Scarecrow believes brains are the only things worth having and wants them because he feels like a fool without them. An old crow told him that brains would make him as good as any man and better than some.

l: Dorothy's return to Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IV
s: Dorothy says that people of flesh and blood would rather live in their own homes than in any other country, however beautiful, because there is no place like home.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: Dorothy and the Scarecrow find the Tin Woodman rusted beside a partly chopped tree in the forest and free him by oiling his joints. The Tin Woodman joins them on their journey to the Emerald City, hoping the Great Oz will give him a heart, while the Scarecrow seeks brains and Dorothy wants to return to Kansas. He tells them how the Wicked Witch of the East caused his body parts to be replaced with tin, leaving him without a heart. The companions continue along the road of yellow brick, but Dorothy worries that their bread is nearly gone.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: Dorothy searches for water, finds the rusted Tin Woodman, and frees him by oiling his joints with the oil-can. She agrees to let him join the journey to the Emerald City and worries that the bread is nearly gone.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The Scarecrow helps Dorothy free the Tin Woodman by gently moving his head and arms after they are oiled. He continues toward the Emerald City to ask the Great Oz for brains and argues that brains are preferable to a heart.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The Tin Woodman is found rusted in place after standing in the forest for more than a year. Once Dorothy and the Scarecrow oil his joints, he can move again, joins their party, and explains that he wants the Great Oz to give him a heart.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The Great Oz is the person Dorothy, the Scarecrow, and the Tin Woodman plan to visit in the Emerald City. Dorothy hopes he will send her back to Kansas, the Scarecrow hopes he will provide brains, and the Tin Woodman hopes he will provide a heart.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: Kansas is the place Dorothy wants the Great Oz to send her back to.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The Emerald City is the destination toward which Dorothy, the Scarecrow, and the Tin Woodman travel to seek help from the Great Oz.

l: the Wicked Witch of the East, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The Wicked Witch of the East was promised two sheep and a cow to prevent the Tin Woodman from marrying the Munchkin girl. She enchanted his axe so that it successively cut off his legs, arms, head, and body, leaving him without a heart.

l: Munchkin girl, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The Munchkin girl was beautiful, loved the Tin Woodman, and promised to marry him once he earned enough money to build a better house. After he lost his heart, the Tin Woodman believed she was still living with the old woman and waiting for him.

l: forest, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The forest contains the cottage, a spring, and the tree beside which the Tin Woodman has rusted. Dorothy, the Scarecrow, and the Tin Woodman travel through it before reaching the road of yellow brick.

l: the road of yellow brick, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The road of yellow brick is the route followed by Dorothy and her companions toward the Emerald City. The Tin Woodman clears a blocked section of it with his axe.

l: jeweled oil-can (Tin Woodman's oil-can), The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The oil-can is found on a shelf in the Tin Woodman's cottage and is used to free his rusted neck, arms, and legs. Dorothy places it in her basket so it can be used again if rain causes him to rust.

l: axe, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The axe once enchanted by the Wicked Witch of the East repeatedly cut off the Tin Woodman's body parts. After he is rescued, he carries it and uses it to clear branches blocking the road.

l: brains, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: Brains are what the Scarecrow wants the Great Oz to give him. The Tin Woodman believes that brains do not make a person happy and would rather have a heart.

l: heart, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: The Tin Woodman lost his heart when his body was replaced with tin, and he consequently lost his love for the Munchkin girl. He believes a heart is the key to happiness and plans to ask the Great Oz for one.

l: Tin Woodman's rescue, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter V
s: Dorothy and the Scarecrow rescue the Tin Woodman after hearing his groans and finding him unable to move because his joints have rusted. They oil and loosen his joints, allowing him to lower his axe, walk, and join their journey.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: Dorothy, Toto, the Scarecrow, and the Tin Woodman encounter a Lion in the forest, and Dorothy calls him a coward after he attacks her companions and threatens Toto. The Cowardly Lion admits that he lacks courage and joins the group so Oz can give him courage. During the journey, the Tin Woodman accidentally kills a beetle, cries, and rusts his jaws until the Scarecrow oils them. The companions continue toward the Emerald City, where they hope Oz will grant their wishes.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: Dorothy protects Toto by rushing at the Lion and slapping his nose when he tries to bite the dog. She calls the Lion a coward, then welcomes him into the group when he decides to ask Oz for courage. She continues toward the Emerald City to ask Oz to send her and Toto back to Kansas.

l: Toto, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: Toto stays close to Dorothy when the forest animals growl and runs barking toward the Lion when he becomes an enemy. Dorothy protects him from being bitten, and he later becomes good friends with the Cowardly Lion.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: The Lion knocks the Scarecrow spinning to the edge of the road, but Dorothy picks him up and pats him back into shape. The Scarecrow says he is going to ask Oz for brains because his head is stuffed with straw. He oils the Tin Woodman's jaws after they rust shut.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: The Lion's claws cannot harm the Tin Woodman, though the attack knocks him down. He says he will ask Oz for a heart and explains that he believes he cannot have heart disease because he has no heart. After accidentally killing a beetle, he cries, rusts his jaws shut, and becomes more careful not to harm living creatures.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: The Cowardly Lion attacks the group but admits that he is a coward after Dorothy confronts him. He explains that he frightens animals by roaring but becomes afraid whenever there is danger. He joins the journey to ask Oz for courage and later becomes good friends with Toto.

l: the little company, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: The little company consists of Dorothy, Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and later the Cowardly Lion. It continues traveling through the forest toward the Emerald City, with the Lion expected to help keep other wild beasts away.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: The Emerald City is the destination of Dorothy and her companions. The country is described as becoming beautiful nearer to the city where Oz dwells.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: Oz is expected to grant the companions' requests. The Scarecrow will ask Oz for brains, the Tin Woodman for a heart, the Cowardly Lion for courage, and Dorothy for a way back to Kansas.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: Kansas is the place Dorothy wants Oz to send her and Toto back to.

l: forest, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: The forest is thick and dangerous, with a yellow brick road covered by branches and dead leaves. Few birds live there, and wild animals growl from among the trees.

l: courage, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: Courage is what the Cowardly Lion believes he lacks and wants Oz to give him. The Scarecrow says Oz could give the Lion courage as easily as brains.

l: cowardice, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: The Cowardly Lion's cowardice makes him unhappy because his heart beats fast whenever there is danger. Although other animals flee from his roar, he still considers himself a coward.

l: heart, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: The Tin Woodman believes he has no heart and plans to ask Oz for one. He suggests that having no heart might prevent someone from being a coward, while his concern over killing a beetle shows his care for living creatures.

l: brains, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: The Scarecrow wants Oz to give him brains because his head is stuffed with straw. He tells the Cowardly Lion that Oz could give him courage as easily as brains.

l: journey to the Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VI
s: The journey leads Dorothy and her companions through a dangerous forest toward the Emerald City. The Cowardly Lion joins the journey, and the group continues peacefully after his arrival.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: Dorothy, the Tin Woodman, the Cowardly Lion, and the Scarecrow continue their journey to the Emerald City through the forest. They cross the first ditch by having the Lion carry them, then use a fallen tree as a bridge over the second gulf and defeat two attacking Kalidahs by chopping the bridge away. After leaving the forest, they reach a broad river and begin building a raft to cross it, but the raft is unfinished when night falls.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: Dorothy camps under a tree, eats the last of her bread, and later gathers nuts and fruit for food. She crosses the first ditch on the Cowardly Lion’s back, helps cross the tree bridge during the Kalidah attack, and becomes tired enough to ride the Lion again. She dreams of the Emerald City and the good Wizard Oz.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The Tin Woodman chops wood for the campfire and later chops down a tree to make a bridge over the second gulf. During the Kalidah attack, he chops away the end of the tree bridge, causing the Kalidahs to fall into the gulf. He begins building a raft to cross the river.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The Cowardly Lion offers to kill a deer for breakfast, then goes into the forest to find his own supper. He carries the Scarecrow, Dorothy, and the Tin Woodman across the first ditch and faces the Kalidahs during their attack. Although he is terrified, he gives a loud roar and is ready to fight before the tree bridge is cut away.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The Scarecrow fills Dorothy’s basket with nuts, helps keep her warm with dry leaves, and proposes that the Cowardly Lion carry them across the first ditch. He suggests using a fallen tree to cross the second gulf and thinks of cutting away the tree bridge when the Kalidahs attack.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The Wizard Oz is the good wizard Dorothy expects to meet in the Emerald City and hopes will send her back to her home.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The Emerald City is the travelers’ destination. Dorothy dreams about reaching it while the group spends the night beside the river.

l: forest, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The travelers camp in the forest, cross a first ditch and a second gulf within it, and encounter the Kalidahs. The forest becomes thick, dark, and gloomy before its trees grow thinner and the travelers reach the river.

l: the road of yellow brick, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The yellow brick road leads the travelers through the forest toward the Emerald City. It crosses the second gulf and continues through the beautiful country on the other side of the river.

l: first ditch, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The first ditch is a wide, deep divide with steep sides and jagged rocks at the bottom. The Cowardly Lion crosses it by carrying the Scarecrow, Dorothy, and the Tin Woodman one at a time.

l: second gulf, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The second gulf is too broad and deep for the Cowardly Lion to jump. The travelers cross it on a tree cut down by the Tin Woodman, but the bridge is later dropped into the gulf to destroy the attacking Kalidahs.

l: Kalidahs, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The Kalidahs are monstrous beasts with bodies like bears, heads like tigers, and long, sharp claws. Two Kalidahs attack the travelers by crossing the tree bridge, but they fall into the gulf when the Tin Woodman chops away its end and are dashed to pieces on the rocks.

l: tree bridge, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The tree bridge is made when the Tin Woodman chops down a tree across the second gulf. The travelers use it to cross, and the Tin Woodman cuts away its near end while two Kalidahs are crossing, causing the bridge and the beasts to fall.

l: river, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The travelers reach a broad river flowing swiftly after leaving the forest. A beautiful country, the yellow brick road, green meadows, flowers, and fruit trees can be seen on the opposite side.

l: the raft, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The raft is proposed as a way to cross the river. The Tin Woodman begins making it from small trees, but it is not finished when night comes.

l: journey to the Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: Dorothy, the Tin Woodman, the Cowardly Lion, and the Scarecrow continue their journey through the forest toward the Emerald City. They overcome two gulfs, survive a Kalidah attack, and reach a river that they must cross.

l: crossing the first ditch, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The Cowardly Lion carries the Scarecrow, Dorothy with Toto, and the Tin Woodman across the first ditch in separate jumps. The crossing succeeds, though the Lion becomes short of breath and needs to rest afterward.

l: Kalidah attack, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: Two Kalidahs attack the travelers while they are crossing the tree bridge over the second gulf. The Lion faces them, but the Scarecrow has the Tin Woodman cut away the bridge, sending both Kalidahs into the gulf.

l: building the raft, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VII
s: The Tin Woodman builds a raft from small trees so the travelers can cross the river. He works industriously, but the raft remains unfinished when the travelers stop for the night.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, the Cowardly Lion, and Toto cross the river on a raft, but the current carries them away from the road of yellow brick, leaving the Scarecrow behind on a pole. A Stork rescues the Scarecrow, and the travelers continue along the riverbank until they enter a meadow of scarlet poppies. The deadly odor puts Dorothy, Toto, and the Cowardly Lion to sleep, while the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman carry Dorothy and Toto out of the poppy field. They place Dorothy safely on grass, but the Lion remains asleep among the poppies because he is too heavy to carry.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: Dorothy crosses the river on the raft with Toto in her arms, but the current carries the group away from the road of yellow brick. She later falls asleep among the poppies, and the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman carry her to safety beside the river.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The Scarecrow is swept away from the raft when his pole sticks in the river mud, leaving him clinging to it in the middle of the water. A Stork carries him back to his friends, after which he helps carry Dorothy out of the poppy field.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The Tin Woodman helps build and steady the raft and uses a pole to push it through the river. He helps rescue the raft, worries about the Scarecrow, and later carries Dorothy with the Scarecrow through the poppies.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The Cowardly Lion helps pull the raft to shore by swimming while the Tin Woodman holds his tail. He runs ahead through the poppy field but eventually falls asleep from the flowers' odor and is too heavy for the others to carry.

l: Stork, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The Stork stops by the river, hears that the Scarecrow is stranded, and carries him from his pole back to the riverbank. She then leaves to return to her babies, wishing the travelers success in reaching the Emerald City.

l: the travelers' party, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The travelers' party crosses the river, is carried downstream away from the road of yellow brick, and reaches the bank with the help of the Cowardly Lion. After the Scarecrow is rescued, the party follows the riverbank and enters the poppy field.

l: river, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The river has a swift current that carries the raft far downstream and away from the road of yellow brick. It leaves the Scarecrow stranded on a pole until the Stork rescues him.

l: the raft, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The raft is completed from logs fastened with wooden pins and carries Dorothy, Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion across the river. The current sweeps it downstream, and the travelers reach shore after the Lion swims while pulling it.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The travelers are trying to reach the Emerald City, where they hope Oz will help them. The Stork also wishes them success in finding it.

l: the road of yellow brick, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The road of yellow brick leads to the Emerald City, but the river carries the travelers' raft far away from it. The travelers later walk along the riverbank to find the road again.

l: field of poppies, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The travelers enter a great meadow of poppies after the other flowers become fewer. The field puts Dorothy, Toto, and the Cowardly Lion to sleep, while the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman carry Dorothy and Toto beyond its dangerous scent.

l: poppies, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The poppies are large, scarlet flowers whose powerful odor causes anyone who breathes it to fall asleep. Their flowers cover a great meadow and are too strong for Dorothy, Toto, and the Cowardly Lion.

l: the deadly poppy odor, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The deadly poppy odor makes Dorothy's eyes grow heavy and causes her to fall asleep, while Toto also falls asleep. It nearly overcomes the Cowardly Lion, but it does not trouble the Scarecrow or the Tin Woodman because they are not made of flesh.

l: sleep caused by the poppies, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: Sleep caused by the poppies can continue forever if the sleeper is not moved away from the flowers' scent. Dorothy and Toto are carried away from the poppies, but the Cowardly Lion remains asleep in the field.

l: the Scarecrow's rescue, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The Scarecrow's rescue is carried out by a Stork after the raft leaves him clinging to a pole in the river. The Stork grabs him by the arm, carries him to the bank, and returns him to Dorothy, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion.

l: the raft crossing, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter VIII
s: The raft crossing begins successfully, with the Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow using poles to push the raft through the water. The current becomes too strong in the middle of the river, carrying the raft downstream and separating the Scarecrow from the others.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The Tin Woodman kills a Wildcat that is chasing the Queen of all the Field Mice and saves her life. In gratitude, the Queen orders thousands of field mice to help rescue the Cowardly Lion from the poppy bed. Using strings and a truck made by the Tin Woodman, the mice pull the sleeping Lion to safety. Dorothy, the Scarecrow, and the Tin Woodman wait beside the rescued Lion while he sleeps.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: Dorothy wakes and is astonished to find thousands of field mice around her. She meets the Queen of all the Field Mice, thanks the mice for rescuing the Cowardly Lion, eats fruit brought by the Scarecrow, and holds Toto tightly so he will not chase the Queen.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The Scarecrow suggests that the field mice rescue the Cowardly Lion from the poppy bed. He asks the Queen to summon thousands of mice with strings and helps the Tin Woodman move the Lion onto the truck.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The Tin Woodman kills the Wildcat with his axe and saves the Queen of all the Field Mice. He protects the mice from Toto, builds a truck from tree limbs and pieces of a tree trunk, and helps push the loaded truck out of the poppy bed.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The Cowardly Lion is asleep in the poppy bed and is in danger from the poisonous scent of the flowers. The field mice pull him out on a truck to the green fields, where he can breathe fresh air, and he remains asleep afterward.

l: Queen of all the Field Mice, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The Queen of all the Field Mice is chased by a Wildcat until the Tin Woodman saves her. She orders thousands of field mice to help rescue the Cowardly Lion and promises to come to the group's assistance if they call for her again.

l: field mice, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The field mice obey their Queen, bring pieces of string, and harness themselves to the truck. Thousands of them pull the Cowardly Lion out of the poppy bed, then return to their homes.

l: Wildcat, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The Wildcat chases the Queen of all the Field Mice with its teeth exposed and its red eyes glowing. The Tin Woodman cuts its head clean off with his axe.

l: field of poppies, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The poppy bed is where the Cowardly Lion lies asleep, and its poisonous scent threatens to keep him from waking. The Lion is carried out of it to the green fields.

l: truck, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The Tin Woodman makes the truck from tree limbs, wooden pegs, and pieces of a tree trunk. The field mice pull it with the Cowardly Lion, the Scarecrow, and the Tin Woodman aboard.

l: strings, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The field mice each bring a long piece of string. The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman use the strings to tie the mice to the truck so they can pull it.

l: Wildcat's attack on the field mouse, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The Wildcat's attack pursues the Queen of all the Field Mice across the grass and threatens her life. The attack ends when the Tin Woodman cuts the Wildcat's head off.

l: Tin Woodman's rescue of the Queen, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The Tin Woodman's rescue of the Queen saves her from the Wildcat. In return, the Queen declares that her people must serve the Tin Woodman and obey his slightest wish.

l: rescue of the Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter IX
s: The rescue of the Cowardly Lion is organized by the Scarecrow and carried out by thousands of field mice. They harness themselves to the Tin Woodman's truck and pull the Lion from the poisonous poppy bed into the fresh air.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: Dorothy, the Cowardly Lion, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and Toto resume their journey along the road of yellow brick toward the Emerald City. They spend a night with a family in the Land of Oz and learn that the Great Oz is difficult to see and may take many forms. At the Emerald City gate, the Guardian of the Gates warns them about Oz and fits each traveler with locked green spectacles before leading them into the city toward the Palace.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: Dorothy resumes the journey with her companions and asks a farmhouse family for food and a place to sleep. She wants the Great Oz to send her back to Kansas, reaches the Emerald City, and is fitted with locked green spectacles before entering the city.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: The Cowardly Lion awakens safely after the field mice rescue him from the poppies. He travels with Dorothy and the others, guards Dorothy’s room overnight, and is fitted with locked green spectacles at the Emerald City gate.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: The Scarecrow travels with Dorothy toward the Emerald City and wants the Great Oz to give him brains. He argues that their errand is important and is fitted with locked green spectacles before entering the city.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: The Tin Woodman travels with Dorothy toward the Emerald City and wants the Great Oz to give him a heart. He is fitted with locked green spectacles at the city gate.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: The Great Oz is described as a powerful and terrible wizard who rules the Emerald City wisely and well but usually does not allow anyone to see him. He is said to take any form, including a bird, elephant, cat, beautiful fairy, or brownie, and to possess brains, hearts, and courage that he may give to the travelers.

l: Guardian of the Gates, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: The Guardian of the Gates meets Dorothy and her companions at the Emerald City gate. He warns them that Oz may destroy those who approach dishonestly or from curiosity, fits them with locked green spectacles, and leads them through another gate toward the Palace.

l: Land of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: The travelers enter a green region of the Land of Oz where fences, houses, clothing, and the people’s skin have green coloring. The people are less friendly than the Munchkins and are afraid of the Cowardly Lion.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: The Emerald City is surrounded by a high, thick, bright green wall and has streets and rooms that glisten with emeralds. Its people wear green spectacles day and night because Oz ordered them to do so, and the Guardian of the Gates leads the travelers into the city.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: Kansas is Dorothy’s home, although she does not know where it is. Dorothy wants the Great Oz to send her back there.

l: gate (Emerald City), The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: The Emerald City gate stands at the end of the road of yellow brick and is studded with glittering emeralds. A bell opens it, allowing Dorothy and her companions to enter a high arched room, and the Guardian later opens another gate leading into the city streets.

l: spectacles (Emerald City), The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: The spectacles have green glasses and are required because the brightness and glory of the Emerald City could blind anyone without them. The Guardian of the Gates fits spectacles to Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, the Cowardly Lion, and Toto, then locks them on with golden bands and a key.

l: Palace of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: The Great Oz sits day after day in the great Throne Room of his Palace and does not allow people to see him face to face. The Guardian of the Gates leads Dorothy and her companions toward the Palace after they enter the Emerald City.

l: journey to the Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: Dorothy and her companions find the road of yellow brick again and continue toward the Emerald City. They pass through the green country, spend a night at a farmhouse, reach the city wall, and enter the city under the Guardian of the Gates’ direction.

l: visit to the Great Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion seek the Great Oz to obtain a way home, brains, a heart, and courage. They are warned that seeing Oz is difficult, but the Guardian of the Gates agrees to take them to his Palace.

l: Dorothy's return to Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter X
s: Dorothy hopes that the Great Oz will find Kansas and send her there because it is her home. In this unit, she has not yet returned to Kansas.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: Dorothy and her companions enter the green City of Oz and are lodged in the Palace of Oz while waiting to see the Great Wizard. Oz appears to each visitor in a different form and promises to grant Dorothy's request to return home, the Scarecrow's desire for brains, the Tin Woodman's desire for a heart, and the Lion's desire for courage only after the Wicked Witch of the West is killed. The companions agree to travel to the land of the Winkies and destroy the Witch, then prepare to leave the next morning.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: Dorothy enters the City of Oz with Toto and her companions and receives a comfortable green room in the Palace of Oz. She asks Oz to send her back to Kansas to Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, but Oz requires her to kill the Wicked Witch of the West first. Although she does not want to kill anyone, she agrees to travel with her friends to confront the Witch.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The Scarecrow is lodged in a Palace room but stands awake all night watching a spider because he cannot lie down or close his eyes. Oz promises to give him many brains and make him the wisest man in the Land of Oz if he helps kill the Wicked Witch of the West. He agrees to accompany Dorothy despite believing he will be of little help.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The Tin Woodman spends the night moving his joints to keep them in working order because he cannot sleep. Oz promises to give him the biggest, kindest, and most loving heart in the Land of Oz after the Wicked Witch of the West is killed. He agrees to go with Dorothy, saying that he has no heart to harm even a Witch.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The Cowardly Lion asks Oz for courage, but Oz requires proof that the Wicked Witch of the West is dead before granting it. After seeing Oz as an intensely hot Ball of Fire, the Lion retreats in fear and tells his friends that they must seek out and destroy the Witch. He agrees to go with them despite being too cowardly to kill her.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: Oz receives Dorothy and her companions one at a time and appears to them as a gigantic Head, a winged Lady, a terrible Beast, and a Ball of Fire. He refuses to grant their requests until the Wicked Witch of the West is killed, though he promises Dorothy a way home, the Scarecrow brains, the Tin Woodman a heart, and the Lion courage. Oz does not allow the visitors to see him together and demands that they not return until their task is completed.

l: Wicked Witch of the West, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The Wicked Witch of the West is described by Oz as the only Wicked Witch left in the land. Oz orders Dorothy and her companions to kill her before he will grant their wishes, and they decide to travel to the land of the Winkies to seek her out.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The City of Oz is filled with green marble buildings, emeralds, green glass, green-tinted skies, and inhabitants dressed in green with greenish skins. Its shops sell green goods, and its people appear happy, contented, and prosperous. The City contains the Palace of Oz at its center.

l: Palace of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The Palace of Oz is a large green building in the middle of the City of Oz, guarded by soldiers and attended by a green girl. Dorothy and her companions are given pleasant rooms there while they wait for their separate audiences with Oz. The Palace includes the Throne Room where Oz appears in different forms.

l: Land of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The Land of Oz is described as beautiful, though Dorothy says she does not like the country and wants to return to Kansas. Oz says that the Land of Oz has only one Wicked Witch left. The companions plan to travel to the land of the Winkies, a part of the Land of Oz, to find her.

l: Throne Room, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The Throne Room is a large round chamber whose walls, ceiling, and floor are covered with emeralds. A bright light in the roof makes the emeralds sparkle, and a green marble throne stands in the center. Oz receives each visitor there while taking a different form.

l: Silver Shoes, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: Dorothy tells Oz that she received the silver shoes from the Wicked Witch of the East when her house fell on and killed the Witch. Oz is very interested in the shoes and says that they bear a powerful charm.

l: destruction of the Wicked Witch of the West, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The death of the Wicked Witch of the West is made the condition for every requested favor. Dorothy and her companions decide that they must destroy the Witch and bring Oz proof that she is dead.

l: Dorothy's return to Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: Dorothy wants Oz to send her back to Kansas, where Aunt Em and Uncle Henry are. Oz refuses to help her return until she kills the Wicked Witch of the West, so she prepares to travel with her companions to seek out the Witch.

l: brains, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The Scarecrow asks Oz to replace the straw in his head with brains so that he can become as much a man as anyone in Oz. Oz promises him many brains and wisdom beyond that of anyone else in the Land of Oz if he helps kill the Wicked Witch of the West.

l: the Tin Woodman's desire for a heart, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The Tin Woodman asks Oz for a heart because he cannot love and wants to be like other men. Oz promises to give him a large, kind, and loving heart after the Wicked Witch of the West is killed.

l: courage, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XI
s: The Cowardly Lion asks Oz to give him courage so that he can truly become the King of Beasts. Oz tells him that he will receive courage when the Lion brings proof that the Wicked Witch of the West is dead.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: Dorothy and her companions leave the Emerald City and travel west into the country of the Winkies to find the Wicked Witch of the West. The Witch sends wolves, crows, bees, Winkies, and finally the Winged Monkeys against them, but the Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, Cowardly Lion, and the Good Witch’s protection help them survive. The Winged Monkeys capture the Tin Woodman, Scarecrow, and Lion and carry Dorothy to the Witch’s castle, where Dorothy is forced to work and secretly feeds the Lion. After the Witch steals one of Dorothy’s Silver Shoes, Dorothy throws water on her, causing the Wicked Witch of the West to melt away.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: Dorothy leaves the Emerald City and travels west with her companions to find the Wicked Witch of the West. The Winged Monkeys carry her safely to the Witch’s castle because the mark of the Good Witch’s kiss protects her. She is forced to work in the castle, secretly feeds the Cowardly Lion, and finally melts the Witch with a bucket of water.

l: Toto, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: Toto travels with Dorothy and is protected from the bees by the Scarecrow’s straw. The Winged Monkeys do not harm him while carrying Dorothy to the Witch’s castle. He stays with Dorothy during her captivity and becomes unhappy when she is unhappy.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Scarecrow keeps watch while Dorothy, Toto, and the Cowardly Lion sleep, and he defeats forty wild crows by twisting their necks. He protects Dorothy and the others from the bees by having his straw spread over them. The Winged Monkeys pull all the straw from him and throw his clothes, hat, and boots into a tall tree.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Tin Woodman keeps watch and kills forty wolves with his axe. He protects Dorothy and the others from the bees because their stings break against his tin body. The Winged Monkeys carry him over sharp rocks and drop him, leaving him battered and dented so that he cannot move or groan.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Cowardly Lion travels with Dorothy and helps frighten away the Winkies sent to attack them. The Winged Monkeys tie him with rope and take him to the Witch’s castle, where he is kept in a fenced yard. Dorothy secretly brings him food each night, and he refuses to be harnessed like a horse.

l: Wicked Witch of the West, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Wicked Witch of the West watches Dorothy and her companions with one eye as powerful as a telescope and sends various forces to destroy or capture them. She uses the Golden Cap’s final summons to call the Winged Monkeys, then enslaves Dorothy and tries to steal both Silver Shoes. She is afraid of water, and Dorothy causes her to shrink and melt by throwing water over her.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Emerald City is left far behind when Dorothy and her companions travel west toward the Wicked Witch of the West. Dorothy’s dress and Toto’s ribbon, which appeared green in the city, become white after they leave.

l: the land of the Winkies, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The country of the Winkies lies west of the Emerald City and has no farms or houses, with rough, hilly, untilled ground. The Wicked Witch of the West rules it, and the Winkies living there are her slaves.

l: castle of the Wicked Witch, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The castle of the Wicked Witch is where Dorothy is taken after the Winged Monkeys capture her companions. Dorothy is made to clean the kitchen and perform other work there, while the Cowardly Lion is confined in a fenced courtyard. Dorothy becomes free to leave the castle after the Witch melts away.

l: Winkies, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Winkies are the slaves of the Wicked Witch of the West and are forced to obey her commands. A dozen Winkies are sent to destroy Dorothy and her companions, but they flee when the Cowardly Lion roars and charges. The Witch beats them when they return and later keeps the castle guarded by yellow Winkies.

l: Winged Monkeys, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Winged Monkeys are summoned for the third and final time by the Wicked Witch’s Golden Cap. They batter and disable the Tin Woodman, strip the straw from the Scarecrow, tie up the Cowardly Lion, and carry Dorothy to the Witch’s castle. They do not harm Dorothy or Toto because Dorothy is protected by the Power of Good, and their service to the Witch ends after this command.

l: Golden Cap, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Golden Cap has a circle of diamonds and rubies and allows its owner to summon the Winged Monkeys three times. The Wicked Witch used it first to enslave the Winkies and second to drive the Great Oz out of the western land. She uses its final summons to attack Dorothy and her companions.

l: Silver Shoes, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Silver Shoes belong to Dorothy and possess a powerful charm. The Wicked Witch fears their power and steals one shoe by making Dorothy trip over an invisible iron bar. Dorothy retrieves the shoe after the Witch melts and puts it back on her foot.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: Kansas is the place Dorothy longs to return to with Aunt Em. During her captivity, Dorothy becomes sad because she thinks it will be harder than ever to get back there.

l: the charm of the Golden Cap, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Golden Cap charm permits its owner to command the Winged Monkeys three times, but no more. The Wicked Witch has already used it twice before this unit and uses the third and final command to capture Dorothy’s companions and bring Dorothy to her castle.

l: journey to the Wicked Witch, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: Dorothy, Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion travel west from the Emerald City into the country of the Winkies. Their journey includes battles against wolves, crows, bees, and Winkies before the Winged Monkeys separate and capture them.

l: attacks on Dorothy and her companions, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Wicked Witch attacks Dorothy and her companions by sending forty wolves, forty crows, a swarm of black bees, a dozen Winkies, and finally the Winged Monkeys. The Tin Woodman defeats the wolves and survives the bees, the Scarecrow defeats the crows, and the Cowardly Lion frightens away the Winkies. The Winged Monkeys succeed in disabling the Tin Woodman and Scarecrow, imprisoning the Lion, and carrying Dorothy to the Witch’s castle.

l: destruction of the Wicked Witch of the West, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XII
s: The Wicked Witch of the West melts after Dorothy throws a bucket of water over her. The Witch shrinks and falls apart into a brown, shapeless mass, and Dorothy sweeps away what remains before recovering the Silver Shoe.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: Dorothy and the Cowardly Lion free the Winkies after the Wicked Witch is melted, then lead a rescue of the Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow. The Winkies repair the Tin Woodman and restore the Scarecrow with clean straw. After several happy days at the Yellow Castle, Dorothy and her friends decide to return to Oz to claim his promise. The Winkies give the travelers gifts, and the group begins the journey to the Emerald City.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: Dorothy unlocks the Cowardly Lion's prison, declares the Winkies free, and organizes the rescue of the Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow. She helps care for her friends, thinks of Aunt Em, and leads the decision to return to Oz and claim his promise. Before leaving, she takes the Golden Cap, accepts a diamond-studded bracelet from the Winkies, and starts for the Emerald City.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: The Cowardly Lion is freed from prison after the Wicked Witch is melted. He helps Dorothy rescue the Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow, then prepares to return to Oz to obtain his courage. The Winkies give him a golden collar.

l: Wicked Witch of the West, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: The Wicked Witch has been melted by a bucket of water. Her castle and cupboard remain available to Dorothy and her friends, and Dorothy finds the Golden Cap in the cupboard.

l: Winkies, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: The Winkies are freed from slavery and celebrate their emancipation with feasting and dancing. They help rescue and repair the Tin Woodman and recover the Scarecrow, then give gifts and good wishes to Dorothy and her companions before they leave.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: The Tin Woodman is found battered and bent on a rocky plain, with his rusted axe nearby. Winkie tinsmiths repair him over three days and four nights, and a goldsmith gives his axe a solid-gold handle and polishes its blade. He rejoins Dorothy and the others and prepares to return to Oz to obtain his heart.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: The Scarecrow's clothes are found in the branches of a tall tree after the Winged Monkeys have tossed them there. Dorothy has the clothes stuffed with clean straw, restoring the Scarecrow, who rejoins the group and plans to return to Oz to obtain his brains. The Winkies give him a gold-headed walking stick.

l: Aunt Em, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: Dorothy thinks of Aunt Em while staying at the Yellow Castle and decides that she must return to Oz.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: Oz is the person whose promise Dorothy and her friends intend to claim when they return to the Emerald City.

l: castle of the Wicked Witch, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: The Yellow Castle becomes a place of freedom and celebration for the Winkies and a refuge for Dorothy and her friends. The Tin Woodman is repaired there, and the Scarecrow is restored there before the group leaves.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: The Emerald City is the travelers' destination after they leave the Yellow Castle. They plan to go there to meet Oz and claim his promise.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: Kansas is the place Dorothy hopes to return to after Oz fulfills his promise.

l: the rescue, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: The rescue frees the Winkies from the Wicked Witch's rule and brings the Cowardly Lion out of prison. It also recovers the battered Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow's clothes, leading to the restoration of both friends.

l: the Winkies' emancipation, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: Dorothy announces that the Winkies are no longer slaves after the Wicked Witch is melted. The Winkies rejoice, make the day a holiday, and remain grateful to Dorothy for freeing them.

l: the Tin Woodman's repair, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: Winkie tinsmiths straighten the Tin Woodman, repair his broken parts, and restore the movement of his joints. They leave several patches, which he does not mind, and his axe is later fitted with a solid-gold handle and polished blade.

l: journey to the Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: After spending several days at the Yellow Castle, Dorothy and her friends begin their journey to the Emerald City. The Winkies say goodbye, give them gifts, and send them off with three cheers and good wishes.

l: the promise to the travelers, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIII
s: Dorothy and her friends decide to return to Oz and claim his promise. The Tin Woodman expects to receive a heart, the Scarecrow expects brains, the Cowardly Lion expects courage, and Dorothy hopes to return to Kansas.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, the Cowardly Lion, and Toto lose their way while traveling through the great fields toward the Emerald City. The Queen of the Mice tells Dorothy to use the Golden Cap to summon the Winged Monkeys, who carry the travelers to the city. The Monkey King explains that the Winged Monkeys are bound to obey the owner of the Golden Cap three times because of a punishment imposed by Gayelette. The Winged Monkeys leave the travelers safely at the Emerald City.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: Dorothy travels with the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, the Cowardly Lion, and Toto through the great fields, but they lose their way. She summons the Winged Monkeys with the Golden Cap, asks them to carry the group to the Emerald City, and learns the history of their binding.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The Scarecrow travels with Dorothy and the others through the fields and worries that he will never reach the Emerald City to get his brains. He suggests calling the field mice and is carried by the Winged Monkeys to the city.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The Tin Woodman becomes discouraged during the long journey because he wants to reach Oz and receive his heart. He is carried safely by the Winged Monkeys to the Emerald City.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The Cowardly Lion says that he lacks the courage to keep walking without reaching anywhere. He is carried by the Winged Monkeys to the Emerald City and calls the ride a quick way out of their troubles.

l: Toto, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: Toto becomes too tired to chase a butterfly while the travelers are lost in the fields. A Winged Monkey carries him, although Toto tries to bite it, and he arrives safely at the Emerald City.

l: the travelers' party, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The four travelers try to walk east through the great fields toward the Emerald City but become lost. After Dorothy summons the Winged Monkeys, they are carried safely to the city's gate.

l: Winged Monkeys, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The Winged Monkeys are summoned by Dorothy and carry her companions and Toto through the air to the Emerald City. Their King tells Dorothy that they were once a free, mischievous people and are now bound to obey the owner of the Golden Cap three times.

l: King of the Monkeys, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The Monkey King leads the Winged Monkeys in carrying Dorothy and the others to the Emerald City. He explains that his grandfather caused Quelala's ruined clothing and that Gayelette bound the Winged Monkeys to obey the Golden Cap's owner.

l: Queen of all the Field Mice, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The Queen of the Mice responds to Dorothy's whistle and tells her that the Emerald City is behind them. She explains that the Golden Cap can summon the Winged Monkeys and leaves with the other mice because the Monkeys like to plague them.

l: Wicked Witch of the West, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The Wicked Witch of the West once possessed the Golden Cap and used the Winged Monkeys to enslave the Winkies and drive Oz out of the Land of the West.

l: Gayelette, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: Gayelette was a beautiful and powerful sorceress who used her magic to help people. After the Winged Monkeys ruined Quelala's clothing as a prank, she spared them from drowning but required them to obey the owner of the Golden Cap three times.

l: Quelala, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: Quelala was a handsome, wise, and good young man whom Gayelette transformed into an exceptional man and intended to marry. The Winged Monkeys dropped him into a river, but he swam safely to shore and later pleaded with Gayelette to spare them.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The Emerald City is the travelers' destination and is found to have been behind them while they were lost. The Winged Monkeys carry the travelers there in less than an hour and set them down before its gate.

l: great fields of buttercups and yellow daisies, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The great fields of buttercups and yellow daisies are difficult for the travelers to cross because there is no road or pathway through them. The travelers become lost among the fields and spend several days seeing only scarlet flowers.

l: Golden Cap, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The Golden Cap contains written instructions for a charm that summons the Winged Monkeys. Dorothy uses it to call them, and the Monkey King explains that its owner has three commands over the Winged Monkeys.

l: the charm of the Golden Cap, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The charm of the Golden Cap consists of words written inside the Cap and requires Dorothy to stand on her left foot, right foot, and then both feet while speaking them. It summons the Winged Monkeys to obey the Cap's owner.

l: the three wishes, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The three wishes are the three times that the owner of the Golden Cap may command the Winged Monkeys. The Monkey King says that Dorothy now has the right to lay her wishes upon them.

l: journey to the Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The journey to the Emerald City becomes difficult when the travelers lose their direction in the great fields. The Winged Monkeys shorten the journey by carrying the travelers through the air and setting them down at the city's gate.

l: the Winged Monkeys' binding, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIV
s: The Winged Monkeys' binding began when Gayelette required them to do three times the bidding of the owner of the Golden Cap after they mistreated Quelala. The binding later allowed the Cap's owners to command them, including the Wicked Witch of the West and now Dorothy.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion return to the Emerald City after Dorothy melts the Wicked Witch of the West and demand that Oz fulfill his promises. They discover that Oz is a frightened old man who has used mechanical tricks, disguises, fire, and ventriloquism to appear as different magical beings. Oz admits he is a humbug but agrees to provide the Scarecrow with brains, the Tin Woodman with a heart, and the Lion with courage, while promising to seek a way to send Dorothy back to Kansas. The travelers agree to keep Oz's secret and remain his guests.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: Dorothy returns to the Emerald City with the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion after melting the Wicked Witch of the West. She confronts Oz about his promises and asks how she can get back to Kansas. She agrees to keep his secret while hoping he will find a way to send her home.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: The Scarecrow tells the Guardian of the Gates that the Wicked Witch of the West has been melted and later demands that Oz give him brains. Oz says the Scarecrow is already learning through experience but agrees to stuff his head with brains.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: The Tin Woodman demands the heart Oz promised him and becomes angry when Oz tries to delay fulfilling the promise. After discovering Oz is a humbug, he still agrees to return the next day to receive a heart.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: The Cowardly Lion roars loudly to frighten Oz, accidentally knocking over the screen that hides him. He asks for courage, and Oz explains that he already possesses courage because he faces danger while afraid, but agrees to give him the kind of courage he wants.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: Oz is revealed to be a little old man from Omaha rather than a great wizard. He admits that he is a humbug who used tricks and disguises to appear as a Head, a Lady, a Beast, and a Ball of Fire. He agrees to try to fulfill the travelers' requests and asks them to keep his identity secret.

l: Wicked Witch of the West, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: The Wicked Witch of the West is melted by Dorothy with a bucket of water. Her destruction allows the travelers to return to the Emerald City and claim the promises Oz made.

l: Winged Monkeys, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: The Winged Monkeys are mentioned as beings the Scarecrow threatens to call upon if Oz refuses to receive the travelers. Oz is frightened by this threat because he had previously encountered them in the Land of the West.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: The travelers return to the Emerald City, where the people gather around them after hearing that Dorothy melted the Wicked Witch of the West. Oz explains that the city is not naturally emerald-colored; green spectacles make everything appear green to its inhabitants.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: Kansas is where Dorothy wants to return. She dreams of being there with Aunt Em, and Oz promises to seek a way to carry her over the desert.

l: Palace of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: The travelers are followed by a crowd to the Palace of Oz and are given their old rooms while waiting to see him. Oz offers to treat them as guests in the Palace while he considers how to help Dorothy.

l: Throne Room, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: The travelers enter the Throne Room expecting to see one of Oz's previous forms but initially find it empty. The Lion's roar knocks over a screen there, revealing the little man who has been pretending to be Oz.

l: the promise to the travelers, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: The travelers return to claim Oz's promises after destroying the Wicked Witch of the West. Oz initially tries to delay them, then agrees to provide brains, a heart, and courage and to seek a way to send Dorothy to Kansas.

l: destruction of the Wicked Witch of the West, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: The Wicked Witch of the West is destroyed when Dorothy melts her with water. Oz is surprised and frightened by the news, but the travelers use the destruction as the basis for demanding that he honor his promises.

l: Dorothy's return to Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: Dorothy's return to Kansas remains unresolved in this unit. Oz asks for two or three days to consider how to carry her over the desert and promises to try to find a way.

l: brains, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: Oz tells the Scarecrow that he does not truly need brains because he is gaining knowledge through experience. Nevertheless, Oz promises to stuff the Scarecrow's head with brains and says the Scarecrow must learn to use them himself.

l: heart, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: Oz claims that having a heart often makes people unhappy and suggests that the Tin Woodman is fortunate not to have one. The Tin Woodman rejects this view, and Oz agrees to give him a heart.

l: the Cowardly Lion's courage, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: Oz explains that true courage means facing danger while afraid and says the Cowardly Lion already has that kind of courage. Because the Lion still wants confidence that will make him forget fear, Oz promises to give him courage.

l: Oz's deception, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: Oz's deception consists of using a paper Head suspended by wire, disguises, a structure of skins, a cotton ball soaked in oil, and ventriloquism to appear magical. He has kept himself hidden from his subjects so they would believe he was a powerful wizard.

l: Oz's secret, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XV
s: Oz's secret is that he is not a wizard but an ordinary man and a skilled ventriloquist who became a balloonist. Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion agree not to tell anyone that he is a humbug.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVI
s: The Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, and Cowardly Lion visit Oz to receive the brains, heart, and courage they believe they need. Oz gives the Scarecrow a mixture of bran, pins, needles, and straw, places a silk-and-sawdust heart in the Tin Woodman, and makes the Lion drink a liquid he calls courage. Each is pleased and believes the desired quality has been supplied. Alone, Oz admits that he is a humbug and worries that he cannot send Dorothy back to Kansas.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVI
s: The Scarecrow goes to Oz to receive brains. Oz removes his head, replaces the straw with a mixture of bran, pins, needles, and straw, and tells him he now has bran-new brains. The Scarecrow feels wise and returns proudly to his friends.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVI
s: Dorothy tells the Scarecrow that she has always liked him as he was. She watches curiously after Oz gives him his new brains. Oz later recognizes that returning Dorothy to Kansas will require more than imagination.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVI
s: Oz gives the Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, and Lion substitutes for the qualities they want. He removes the Scarecrow's head, fills it with bran and other materials, puts a silk-and-sawdust heart into the Tin Woodman, and gives the Lion a drink. Alone, Oz admits that he is a humbug and says he does not know how to get Dorothy back to Kansas.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVI
s: The Tin Woodman visits Oz to receive a heart. Oz cuts a square hole in his breast, places a silk heart stuffed with sawdust inside, and solders the tin back together. The Tin Woodman is pleased and grateful despite the patch.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVI
s: The Cowardly Lion goes to Oz to receive courage. Oz pours liquid from a green bottle into a dish and tells the Lion to drink it, explaining that it will be courage once it is inside him. The Lion drinks it and returns joyfully, feeling full of courage.

l: brains, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVI
s: Oz makes the Scarecrow's brains from bran mixed with pins and needles, using straw to fill the remaining space. The Scarecrow believes the mixture has made him wise.

l: heart, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVI
s: Oz's heart for the Tin Woodman is made entirely of silk and stuffed with sawdust. Oz places it in the Tin Woodman's breast and assures him that it is a kind heart.

l: the Cowardly Lion's courage, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVI
s: Oz presents the Lion's courage as liquid from a square green bottle. The Lion drinks it and believes that he is full of courage.

l: humbug, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVI
s: Oz calls himself a humbug because he gives the others things that they imagine fulfill their wishes, even though everyone knows such things cannot truly be made in this way. He is successful in making the Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, and Lion happy, but he does not know how to return Dorothy to Kansas.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: Dorothy, wanting to return to Kansas, helps Oz build a balloon to cross the desert through the air. Oz fills the silk balloon with hot air and attaches a clothes basket, then announces that the Scarecrow will rule the Emerald City while he visits a brother Wizard in the clouds. Dorothy misses the launch while searching for Toto, and Oz rises into the sky without her. The people of the Emerald City mourn Oz but accept the Scarecrow as their ruler.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: Dorothy longs to return to Kansas and helps Oz sew the silk strips for a balloon. She searches for Toto just before the launch and reaches the balloon too late, so she remains behind when Oz departs.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: Oz proposes building a balloon to cross the desert because he does not know which way Kansas lies. He builds and launches the balloon, but it rises before Dorothy can enter, carrying him away from the Emerald City.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: The Scarecrow says he has wonderful thoughts in his head but will not explain them. Oz appoints him to rule the people of the Emerald City during Oz's absence.

l: Toto, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: Toto runs into the crowd to bark at a kitten just before the balloon launch. Dorothy finds him, picks him up, and runs toward the balloon, but they arrive too late.

l: people of the Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: The people come to watch Oz launch the balloon after hearing that he will visit a great brother Wizard in the clouds. They obey Oz's command to accept the Scarecrow as ruler, and they later remember Oz lovingly and grieve over his departure.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: Kansas is the place Dorothy wants to return to. Oz does not know which way Kansas lies, so he first plans to help Dorothy cross the desert.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: The Emerald City is the beautiful city Oz built for its people. After Oz leaves, the Scarecrow is left to rule over it.

l: desert, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: The desert lies between Dorothy and the route home that Oz proposes. Oz believes they should cross it through the air, since he thinks traveling by balloon will be safer than crossing it on foot.

l: balloon, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: Oz and Dorothy make a balloon from strips of light green, dark green, and emerald green silk coated with thin glue. A large clothes basket is fastened to it with ropes, but the ropes break during the launch and the balloon rises with Oz alone.

l: hot air, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: Hot air is used to make the balloon float because there is no gas in the country to fill it. Oz explains that hot air is less reliable than gas because the balloon could descend if the air cooled.

l: balloon launch, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: During the launch, the Tin Woodman builds a fire and Oz holds the balloon over it until the balloon swells and lifts the basket. The ropes then crack, sending the balloon upward before Dorothy can board.

l: Oz's departure, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: Oz tells the people that he is going to visit a great brother Wizard in the clouds and leaves the Emerald City in the balloon. Dorothy calls for him to return, but he says he cannot and continues rising into the sky.

l: rule of the Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVII
s: Oz commands the people to obey the Scarecrow as they would obey him while Oz is away. The people accept the Scarecrow as their ruler after Oz's departure.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: Dorothy and her companions mourn Oz's departure, while the Scarecrow becomes ruler of the Emerald City. Dorothy still wants to return to Kansas, but the Winged Monkeys cannot carry her across the desert. The soldier with the green whiskers advises her to seek Glinda, the Witch of the South, whose castle stands near the desert. Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Lion decide to travel to the Land of the South and begin preparing for the journey.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: Dorothy weeps because her hope of returning to Kansas has passed, but she is glad she did not go up in the balloon. She asks the Winged Monkeys to carry her to Kansas, learns that they cannot cross the desert, and decides to seek Glinda's help. She will travel south with the Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, and Lion.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: Oz has gone up in the balloon, causing Dorothy and her companions to mourn his departure. The Tin Woodman remains grateful to Oz for giving him his heart.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: The Tin Woodman mourns Oz and weeps while Dorothy wipes away his tears so he will not rust. He is pleased with his new heart and agrees to accompany Dorothy south, bringing his axe.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: The Scarecrow becomes the ruler of the Emerald City, and its people are proud that a stuffed man rules them. He suggests calling the Winged Monkeys and later recommends that Dorothy travel south to ask Glinda for help. He decides to accompany Dorothy because she helped him gain his brains and good fortune.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: The Lion is content to know that he is as brave as any beast, if not braver. He decides to leave the Emerald City and travel with Dorothy because he longs for the woods and country and wants to protect her.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: The Emerald City and its Palace belong to the Scarecrow after Oz's departure. The Scarecrow rules the city, and its people are proud of him.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: Kansas is where Dorothy wants to return so she can live with Aunt Em and Uncle Henry. The Winged Monkeys cannot carry her there because they belong only to their own country.

l: Winged Monkeys, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: The Winged Monkeys answer Dorothy's second call and enter the Throne Room. Their king tells her that they cannot leave their country or cross the desert to Kansas, so they fly away without helping her.

l: Golden Cap, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: Dorothy brings out the Golden Cap and uses its magic words to call the Winged Monkeys. She believes she has wasted its charm when they cannot help her reach Kansas.

l: Glinda, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: Glinda is the Witch of the South and is said to be the most powerful of all the Witches. She rules the Quadlings, is kind to everyone, and has a castle on the edge of the desert, so she may know how Dorothy can cross it.

l: Land of the South, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: The Land of the South is where Glinda rules the Quadlings. Dorothy and all three companions decide to travel there despite the dangers along the road.

l: desert, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: The desert lies between Dorothy and Kansas, and nobody is known to have crossed it except possibly Oz. Glinda's castle stands on its edge, and the Winged Monkeys cannot cross it.

l: balloon, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: The balloon goes up with Oz, taking him away from the Emerald City. Dorothy is glad she did not use it to try to return to Kansas.

l: journey to the South, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: The journey to the South is chosen as the best way for Dorothy to find help in returning to Kansas. It is expected to be long and dangerous, and the companions plan to begin it the next morning.

l: hope of returning to Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XVIII
s: Dorothy's hope of returning to Kansas seems to pass when Oz leaves in the balloon. She continues seeking a way home and places new hope in finding Glinda in the South.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: Dorothy, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Lion leave the Emerald City and continue their journey toward the Land of the South so Dorothy can return to Kansas. They pass through green fields and a thick forest whose first-row trees attack them, but the Tin Woodman cuts branches so the group can proceed. At the far edge of the forest, they encounter a high, smooth wall made of white china, and the Tin Woodman decides to make a ladder to climb over it.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: Dorothy says farewell to the Guardian of the Gate and expresses gratitude for how kindly she was treated in the Emerald City. She travels toward the Land of the South with her companions, hoping to return to Kansas, and helps pick up the Scarecrow after the trees throw him.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: The Scarecrow is told that he is now the ruler of the Emerald City, but he leaves with Dorothy to help her get home. In the forest, the fighting trees seize him with their branches and throw him, though he is not hurt.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: The Tin Woodman leaves the Emerald City with Dorothy and the others. He chops through a branch of a fighting tree, allowing the group to pass, frees Toto from another branch, and later decides to make a ladder to climb over the white china wall.
